title: Remove Interval
statement:
`intervals` describes a set of real numbers. It is a list of pairs sorted by their first value that never overlap, and a pair `[a, b]` stands for the half-open range of every real `x` with `a <= x < b`. `toBeRemoved` is one more half-open range in the same format.

Return the numbers that lie in the set but not in `toBeRemoved`, written the same way: a list of pairs sorted by their first value.

- Cut each input pair on its own: it keeps the part of it before `toBeRemoved` and the part after it, each only when that part is non-empty.
- Never join pieces that come from different input pairs, even when one ends exactly where the next begins.
- When nothing is left, return an empty list.
constraints: -10^9 <= a < b <= 10^9 for every pair [a, b], including toBeRemoved
intervals is sorted by start and no two of its ranges overlap (one may end where the next starts)
notes:
## Intuition

Each input range is affected by the removal independently, because the ranges never overlap. A range either misses `toBeRemoved` entirely and survives as it is, or it overlaps it, and then at most two pieces survive: the bit before the removed range and the bit after it. Since the input is already sorted, emitting those pieces in input order keeps the answer sorted. A brute force could cut the number line at every endpoint and test each tiny segment, but one pass over the ranges is enough.

## Approach

1. Unpack `toBeRemoved` into `removeStart` and `removeEnd`.
2. For each `[start, end]`: if it ends at or before `removeStart`, or starts at or after `removeEnd`, push it unchanged.
3. Otherwise it overlaps. If `start < removeStart`, keep the left piece `[start, removeStart]`.
4. If `end > removeEnd`, keep the right piece `[removeEnd, end]`.
5. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

`toBeRemoved = [1, 6]`, so `removeStart = 1`, `removeEnd = 6`.
- `[0, 2]` overlaps. `0 < 1` keeps `[0, 1]`; `2 > 6` is false, so no right piece.
- `[3, 4]` overlaps and lies inside the removal: `3 < 1` and `4 > 6` are both false, so nothing survives.
- `[5, 7]` overlaps. `5 < 1` is false; `7 > 6` keeps `[6, 7]`.

`result` is `[[0, 1], [6, 7]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), one look at each range.
- Space: O(1) besides the output, which holds at most n + 1 pairs.

## Pitfalls

- The ranges are half-open, so a range ending exactly at `removeStart` does not overlap it: use `<=` and `>=` in the "no overlap" test.
- A range that covers `toBeRemoved` on both sides splits into two pieces; checking the two sides with separate `if`s (not `else if`) handles it.
- Do not merge touching ranges such as `[0, 2]` and `[2, 4]`; each input range keeps its own pieces.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `removeStart`, `removeEnd` | the bounds of the range to delete |
| `start`, `end` | the current input range |
| `result` | the surviving pieces, in sorted order |

narration.2: Name the two bounds of the range we have to delete.
narration.3: Collect the surviving pieces here, in sorted order.
narration.5: Look at each input range once, in its sorted order.
narration.6: Half-open ranges: ending at removeStart or starting at removeEnd means no overlap.
narration.8: Nothing more to do for this range.

narration.11: Keep the left piece, which stops where the removal begins.
narration.13: Does part of the range lie after the removed range?
narration.14: Keep the right piece, which starts where the removal ends.
